title: Driving Ellington bandsmen to the L&N station, c. 1942
summary: He recounts knowing the Ellington band from New York and driving Sonny Greer and Johnny Hodges to the train after a New Orleans concert, with Duke greeting him.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: that ever happened in my life, I'm glad to know that it was 11.30 or 12 o'clock at night. When Duke Ellington, I knew the Duke Ellington band, I knew every guy in the band, because we worked together in New York. I mean, they were upstairs, we were downstairs, we were not in the same band, but every intermission we were together, and Sonny Greer was a dear friend of mine, the drummer, and Roy Eldridge, I knew Roy very well, and they came down here and they played, that's when I first came home, about 1941 or 42, when I came home, before, just before I went into service, 42, and they had a concert at Booker T. Washington Auditorium, and, it was, it was, before I went into service, I went into service in 43, yeah, about 42, I went, they had a concert at the Booker T. Washington Auditorium, and I was gonna go to it, I didn't have a date or anything like that, so I got a fifth of booze, and I went, I got down there a little early, and I went backstage, oh, I went and bought my ticket first, so the best ticket in the house was five dollars, which is in the front rows, downstairs, the orchestra, and it went up to two dollars in the back, figuring that, buying a five dollar ticket, I wouldn't be involved too much with, with black people down in the front, so I went backstage, and they gave them a bottle, and before everybody was having a drink, I even had qualms about drinking out of the same bottle as I called it for all of you, so I, we had a drink, and then after the show was over, I told Senator, oh, well, I had my car, I said, come on, I'll drive you down to this railroad station, you want to go out, anybody else want, yeah, get Sonny, so we got Sonny Greer, and, and the drummer, Sonny, and, the drummer, not Sonny Greer, not, Sonny Greer's the name of the drummer, who's the first alto man?

Johnny Hodges, Johnny Hodges, Johnny, Johnny Hodges and Sonny came with me, and what, so, Sonny always had an affectionate way of walking with you, put his arm around you and he's walking like this and always, even in New York, he used to take me up to Harlem and what, I knew more about Harlem than I knew about Bourbon Street because Sonny used to take me up there and O'Neal Spenter used to take me up there and he used to go up there to get ribs and it was like walking in, in your own living room, you know, you were not scared or nothing and, so we get down to the, get down to the L&N station and park the car and there's Sonny and they're loading up the train right there into the station and they're putting in all the instruments and there's Duke standing there helping to put the instruments in and getting rearranged and so forth. He's walking there,
Duke, Duke, look who's here, look, Son Godfrey's here, Godfrey's here.

I said, Jesus, if somebody sees me with this, I said, I'll be ostracized in New Orleans. Well, it was around 1130, 1230 at 12 o'clock at night and nobody was down there in the railroad station because this was a special train that they had and they were just loading it up there and I saw the guys and I knew the whole band. It was, it was a great gang of guys Ben Webster and the trombone player that wrote Perdido and the whole gang. Was Otto Hardwick
He played alto too. Probably, probably, probably third, third, sixth, third.
